newsitem.title: FRANCE: Channel Tunnel blaze raises safety questions.
newsitem.headline: Channel Tunnel blaze raises safety questions.

text.p: The Franco-British operator of the Channel Tunnel said the link might partly reopen on Wednesday after a blaze on a freight train raised worrying questions about the tunnel's much-vaunted safety.

"The hyper-security was a bluff," railed the French daily France-Soir in a headline after the fire injured eight people on Monday night in a tunnel designed to withstand earthquakes and guerrilla bombs.

Operator Eurotunnel SA Plc said damage was worse than previously feared -- with buckled tracks, cracked concrete and damage to electrical cables -- and repairs are likely to last weeks. The fire started on a train shuttling trucks.
But Eurotunnel aimed quickly to restore partial services on one of the twin 51 km (32-mile) rail tunnels once safety experts gave the green light.

"Technical teams from Eurotunnel have verified that the state of the northern tunnel allows a resumption of traffic on a single track during the day," the company said in a statement after the blaze that injured eight people.
It said it was awaiting approval from the intergovernmental commission overseeing safety, meeting in France on Wednesday.

But the French rail authority SNCF advised passengers hoping to travel through the Channel Tunnel to delay or cancel their trip. Clients have been diverted onto ferries or planes, the tunnel's arch-rivals.
Some Eurostar trains ran to Calais from Paris where passengers disembarked to take ferries.

But the company, already struggling with a mountain of debts and fierce competition from ferries, faced a string of troubling questions about safety after the first major accident since the link opened in 1994.

The train was already ablaze when it entered the tunnel at Calais bound for Britain and, under existing safety guidelines, should have gone straight to the other end at Folkstone when the driver noted the fire, Eurotunnel officials said.

Yet instead of completing the 35-minute trip, a second alarm forced the train to make an emergency halt 18 km (11 miles) inside the tunnel. Rescue services then needed more than 20 minutes to reach the scene of the accident.
The 34 people aboard were forced to use wet napkins over their mouths because there was no breathing gear and ventilation systems prevented fumes from reaching the passenger compartment.
"We don't know what triggered the second alarm," said Eurotunnel spokeswoman Mady Chabrier. "We're investigating." A judicial inquiry was also opened into the accident in France.
The train manager, Emile Grard, who said he had to "improvise" during the rescue, was widely praised for his cool handling of the crisis in France.
"It started with a fire alarm and a call from a British controller," he said. A malfunction on the train meant "we lost control, which led to the halt of the train".
Eurotunnel Chairman Robert Malpas said any inquiry into the accident would examine whether Eurotunnel needed to establish better lines of communication with security and other rail staff.

Also at issue was why the driver was unable to decouple the locomotive and its passenger carriage to drive away from the blazing trucks, which are shipped on open, lattice-sided freight trains criticised as a fire hazard for not being enclosed.
Car shuttles, for instance, have enclosed wagons that can be flooded with halon gas to extinguish any blaze.
Eurotunnel said it would study black boxes for clues.

"We have recordings like the cockpit recorders in a plane so all the communications between the locomotive and the control centre are recorded," said Eurotunnel director-general Georges Christian Chazot.
